open.q: Tell me about yourself
open.probe: The opener. Land on healthcare and real-time voice.
a: Sure. I started out in computer science research at UIC, where I worked on applied ML and LLM systems. That gave me a pretty strong foundation in actually building and evaluating these systems, rather than just using the models.

From there I joined WheelPrice, which was a much more startup-oriented environment. I was working across the stack and got a lot more exposure to shipping things that were actually being used by customers. It was a small engineering team, so I had to be pretty broad — backend, AI, infrastructure, and product work all kind of blended together.

After that I joined alfred_, where I've been working as a founding LLM engineer. It's an AI assistant, and my work has become much more focused on reliability and evaluation — things like building the eval harness, production failure detection, working memory, and making sure agent changes actually improve the product rather than just looking better on a benchmark.

The common thread through all of that has really been building AI systems in environments where you don't have a perfectly defined problem in front of you. You have to figure out what's broken, decide what to build, and then own it through production.

And for the last few months that's meant voice: I own alfred_'s voice agent, which people call from their phones, and before that I built a real-time voice platform on LiveKit from scratch. So an agent that actually answers patients' calls and finishes the job is pretty much where I want to be.

open.q: Why Commure? Why voice agents?
open.probe: After the intro, or after her pitch.
a: A couple of things. From what I read, around 30% of patient calls never get answered, and each one is someone trying to see a doctor. Your agents pick up every call and actually finish the job: they book, reschedule, do intake, and write it back to Epic or Athena. That's a real problem with a real person on the other end.

Second, it's the hardest version of the work I like. Real-time voice, where latency and interruptions matter, plus an agent that takes actions in a system of record, where a wrong booking is worse than no booking. I do exactly that at alfred_: I own our voice agent, phone and web, and it works in people's real email and calendars, where a wrong action is worse than no action.
And healthcare isn't new to me: my research is on multi-agent medical reasoning, and at the UIC lab I worked on voice for patients in the hospital.
So it's a problem I care about, in a domain I've worked in, at a company that's already deployed at scale.

production: If she asks how that maps to EHR write-back: It's the same policy: on the call, the agent can look things up fast, but a write waits for the careful path, gets read back, and the person confirms. For Commure that's a booking in Epic instead of an email.

If she asks how many users: alfred_ has 5,000-plus subscribers, and over a thousand use the phone agent daily. Every call leaves a record with its timing and cost, so we can see what's actually happening.

If she asks about healthcare: My research is multi-agent medical reasoning, TeamMedAgents, and at the UIC lab I deployed an INT8 audio model at 150 milliseconds p95 for patient voice interaction on the hospital network.

open.q: Your voice work: alfred_ first, then MockFlow-AI
open.probe: When she asks what you've done that's closest to the role. Outcome first, then one design choice, then stop.
a: The closest is alfred_'s voice agent, which I own end to end and which is live for everyone. You call alfred_ from your phone, or tap the mic in the web app, and talk to the same assistant that knows your email and calendar. Calls come in over a SIP trunk into LiveKit, the web joins over WebRTC, and one Python worker serves both.

The design choice I'd point to: the agent on the call is deliberately lean, a small set of tools and two quick model calls, so it stays responsive. Every time the caller says something, the same request also goes, in parallel, to our main agent, the one behind chat and SMS. So when a request needs real work, there's no escalation step and no extra two to three seconds of silence. Reads it answers fast; anything that writes waits for the main agent, and the person confirms. It never acts on a half-heard instruction.

Before alfred_, I built MockFlow-AI from scratch: a real-time voice interview platform on LiveKit, under 400 milliseconds end to end, where the conversation moves between stages only when the model calls a tool, so it can't drift. It's live, and it grades its own interviews with a judge I calibrated against human scores.

modules.title: How a call reaches the agent
modules.blurb: Trace a call from the phone network to a Python process holding it, and say why each hop exists.

topics.title: Signalling and media travel apart
topics.brief: A phone call is two flows. SIP sets the call up and tears it down (INVITE, 180 Ringing, 200 OK, BYE) and carries no sound; the audio goes separately as RTP packets over UDP. The nuance people miss: UDP is chosen because late audio is worthless, so a lost 20 ms packet is dropped, never resent.
points: SIP: signalling only; it asks for, rings, answers and ends the call, and carries no audio
RTP: the audio itself, on a separate path, usually over UDP
G.711 mu-law: 8,000 samples a second at 8 bits, 64 kbit/s, cut into 20 ms packets, so 50 packets a second each way
UDP over TCP: a resent packet arrives too late to play, so losing 20 ms beats stalling the stream
SIP trunk: the link between the phone network and your software; the media server turns its packets into an audio track code can read
8 kHz: why phone audio sounds thin, and why speech models on a phone path get narrowband input
production: Twilio Elastic SIP Trunking: origination brings calls from the phone network to your SIP endpoint; termination sends calls out
Twilio Media Streams: another way in, delivering call audio as 8 kHz mu-law over a WebSocket instead of a SIP stack
LiveKit SIP service: terminates the trunk and publishes the caller as a participant with an audio track
Codecs: G.711 on the phone network, Opus on WebRTC; the media server transcodes between them

mcq.q: A caller's audio keeps breaking up, but the call never drops. Which flow is most likely in trouble?
o: The SIP INVITE that set the call up
The SIP BYE that will end the call
The RTP stream carrying the audio packets
The 200 OK that answered the call
The SIP registration of the trunk
mcq.why: Once a call is set up, SIP goes quiet until hang-up. Choppy audio on a live call lives in the RTP media path.

mcq.q: Why does call audio usually travel over UDP rather than TCP?
o: A resent packet would arrive too late to play, so dropping it is better
UDP encrypts the audio and TCP does not
TCP cannot carry binary audio payloads
UDP guarantees packets arrive in order
SIP trunks only accept UDP for signalling
mcq.why: TCP would stall the stream waiting for a resend. In live audio a missing 20 ms is barely heard, a stall is.

mcq.q: What does the 8 kHz sample rate of a phone call mean for a voice agent?
o: The agent has 8 ms to answer each packet
Each packet holds 8,000 samples
The call can carry at most eight participants
Nothing above 4 kHz survives, so speech models get thinner input than on web
Phone audio needs no jitter buffer, unlike web audio
mcq.why: The highest frequency captured is half the sample rate. Models trained on wideband audio lose detail on a phone line.

open.q: A patient dials the clinic. Walk me through what is on the wire before our agent hears the first word.
open.probe: Whether you know what each protocol is for, not only its name.
a: SIP over the trunk sets the call up: INVITE, ringing, 200 OK
Audio flows separately as RTP over UDP, G.711 at 8 kHz, 20 ms packets
UDP because late audio is useless: drop, don't resend
The media server's SIP service turns the packets into an audio track
Trade-off to name: 8 kHz is cheap and universal but costs recognition accuracy

say: I think of a call as two things. SIP sets it up through the trunk: invite, ringing, answer, and later bye. The audio goes separately as RTP over UDP, 20 ms packets, because a late packet is useless, so you drop it rather than wait. On a phone line that audio is 8 kHz, which is why speech models do a bit worse on calls than on the web.
avoid: Saying SIP carries the audio: it only sets the call up and tears it down

topics.title: How a browser joins: WebRTC
topics.brief: A browser can't open raw UDP to anyone it likes, and most users sit behind NAT. WebRTC handles both: an SDP offer and answer describe codecs and addresses, ICE tries candidate paths, STUN finds the public address, and TURN relays as a last resort. The nuance: TURN and the jitter buffer both buy reliability with latency.
points: SDP: the offer and answer saying which codecs and addresses each side supports
ICE: tries candidate paths, a direct address first, then the public address a STUN server reports
TURN: relays every packet when no direct path works (strict NAT, firewalls); costs latency and bandwidth
DTLS-SRTP: WebRTC media is always encrypted
Opus at 48 kHz: the usual web codec, far fuller than a phone line
Jitter buffer: holds a few tens of milliseconds so uneven arrival does not become clicks and gaps
production: LiveKit client SDK: the browser gets a room token from your backend, then connects to the SFU over WebRTC
Signalling is the application's job: WebRTC defines SDP but not how it travels, so LiveKit carries it over its own WebSocket
Adaptive jitter buffers: grow when the network is uneven and shrink when it settles, trading delay for smoothness

mcq.q: A web caller on a strict corporate network only connects through TURN. What changes for that call?
o: The audio switches from Opus to G.711
Every packet goes through a relay, adding latency and bandwidth cost
The media is no longer encrypted
SDP negotiation is skipped
The jitter buffer is switched off
mcq.why: TURN is the fallback relay. The call still works and stays encrypted, but every packet takes the extra hop.

mcq.q: What does a STUN server do in a WebRTC connection?
o: Relays every media packet between the two peers
Encrypts the media stream with SRTP
Carries the SDP offer and answer
Mixes several audio streams into one
Tells a client the public address its NAT presents, so a direct path can be tried
mcq.why: STUN only reports your public address. Relaying is TURN's job; carrying SDP is the signalling channel's.

mcq.q: Why would an engineer accept extra delay from a jitter buffer?
o: It gives the model time to finish generating
It is needed to decrypt DTLS-SRTP
Packets arrive unevenly, and a short hold turns that into smooth playback
It lets the SFU mix streams before forwarding
It lowers the bandwidth Opus needs
mcq.why: Network arrival times vary. A few tens of milliseconds of buffer hides that variation from the listener.

open.q: The patient app gets a 'talk to us' button. What has to happen for that browser to reach our agent, and what goes wrong on a hospital network?
open.probe: NAT traversal and what it costs, in plain words.
a: Backend issues a room token; the browser connects to the media server
SDP offer and answer agree codecs and addresses
ICE tries direct, then STUN's public address, then TURN
Locked-down networks often force TURN: more latency and relay bandwidth
Opus at 48 kHz and a jitter buffer give better audio than the phone line

say: The browser and the server swap SDP, which is pretty much what codecs and addresses each side can use. Then ICE tries paths: direct, then the public address STUN finds, and TURN as a relay if nothing else works. On a locked-down hospital network I'd expect TURN, so a bit more latency. In alfred_ web calls come in over WebRTC into the same kind of room as phone calls.
avoid: Calling STUN a relay: STUN reports your address, TURN relays

topics.title: The agent is a participant in a room
topics.brief: A media server sits between everyone on a call. An MCU decodes and mixes every stream; an SFU forwards packets without decoding. LiveKit is an SFU organised as rooms, and the agent joins as one more participant: it subscribes to the caller's audio and publishes its own. The nuance: the SIP service turns a phone call into a participant too, so one agent serves phone and web.
points: MCU: decodes every stream and mixes them into one; expensive in CPU
SFU: forwards packets without decoding; each participant publishes tracks and subscribes to the ones it wants
Room: one call's space, holding its participants and their tracks
Agent as participant: subscribes to the caller's audio track, publishes its own
Phone and web: both arrive as participants, so the agent code is the same; only codec and sample rate differ
Stateful: a call is pinned to one server for its whole life, unlike a stateless request
production: LiveKit: rooms, participants and tracks are the whole model; the SIP service and the agent framework both join rooms as participants
SFU over MCU: most real-time platforms forward rather than mix, because forwarding needs no decoding
Stateful routing: a live session is pinned to one server, the pattern behind the guide's stateful servers technique

mcq.q: Why can one agent worker serve both phone and web callers?
o: The browser converts its audio to SIP before joining
The phone network supports WebRTC natively
Both arrive as room participants with an audio track, so the agent sees the same thing
The worker runs two code paths behind a flag
The SFU mixes both into one stream for the agent
mcq.why: The SIP service makes the phone caller a participant. From the agent's side a caller is a track to subscribe to, wherever it came from.

mcq.q: An SFU and an MCU both sit in the middle of a call. What does the SFU avoid doing?
o: Decoding and mixing every stream, which costs CPU
Encrypting the media
Keeping any state about the call
Forwarding packets between participants
Grouping participants into rooms
mcq.why: An SFU copies packets to subscribers without decoding them. Mixing is the MCU's expensive step.

mcq.q: Inside a room, how does the agent hear the caller?
o: The SFU posts a mixed audio file to a webhook
The caller's phone streams to the agent's IP over TCP
It polls the media server for new recordings
It reads the audio from the SIP INVITE body
It subscribes to the caller's published audio track
mcq.why: Participants publish tracks and subscribe to others'. The agent is a participant, so it subscribes like anyone else.

open.q: Our agents take phone calls and calls from the patient app. How would you structure that so you don't build two agents?
open.probe: Whether you see the agent as a participant, and where phone and web actually differ.
a: Put every call in a room on an SFU
The SIP service turns a phone call into a participant; the browser joins over WebRTC
The agent joins as a participant: subscribe to the caller, publish its own audio
Differences stay at the edge: 8 kHz G.711 against 48 kHz Opus
Trade-off: one codebase, but test both audio paths, since phone audio is harder for speech models

say: I'd make the agent a participant in a room. The media server turns a phone call from the SIP trunk into a participant, and a browser joins the same kind of room over WebRTC. The agent subscribes to the caller's audio and publishes its own, so it doesn't care where the caller came from. That's how alfred_ runs one worker for phone and web. Only the codec and sample rate differ.
avoid: Describing the agent as a side service the media server calls: it is a participant in the room

topics.title: A call gets a process, not a queue row
topics.brief: Work that can wait goes in a queue: a worker claims a row with SKIP LOCKED, and if it dies another picks the row up later. A call can't wait and can't move: its audio is bound to one process for minutes, with a frame every 20 ms. So the media server pushes the call to a worker with spare capacity, which runs it in its own process. The nuance: capacity is CPU per call, so you scale out by adding workers.
points: Pull: a worker claims a job row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; fine for work that can wait and retry
Push: when a room is created, the dispatcher hands the job to a registered worker with spare capacity
One job, one process: each call runs in its own child process for its whole life
No moving a call: if that process dies, the live call loses its agent; nothing replays it later
Capacity: CPU, because voice activity, turn detection and audio handling run per call
Scale out: more worker containers, with the dispatcher balancing new calls across them
production: LiveKit agent dispatch: a SIP dispatch rule creates a room per inbound call and dispatches the named agent into it
LiveKit server options: each job runs in its own process; prewarm loads models before the first job; a load threshold stops new jobs when a server is busy
Postgres SKIP LOCKED: the pull side, enough for many job queues without a separate broker

mcq.q: An SMS reply and a phone call both reach your backend. Why queue one and dispatch the other?
o: SMS needs a database and calls do not
The SMS can wait and be retried from a row; the call is a live stream pinned to one process
Call audio is too large to store in a Postgres row
Queues cannot run more than one worker at a time
SKIP LOCKED does not work for audio data
mcq.why: Pull suits work that tolerates delay and retry. A call needs a process now and for its whole length.

mcq.q: What most limits how many calls one worker container can hold?
o: Disk space for recordings
The number of SIP trunks
CPU, because voice activity, turn detection and audio run per call
Database connections per call
The model provider's context window
mcq.why: Each call is a process doing audio work every 20 ms. That CPU load is what you load-test per container.

mcq.q: A worker crashes in the middle of its work. How does a live call differ from a queued job?
o: The call loses its agent; the job's lease expires and another worker retries it
Both are retried by another worker from the start
The call moves to another worker without the caller noticing
The job is lost and the call is retried
Neither is affected, because state is in Postgres
mcq.why: A job's state lives in a row, so it survives the worker. A call's state is the live stream in that process.

open.q: Why not put incoming calls on a job queue like the rest of our background work?
open.probe: Push against pull, and the backend reasoning behind a voice system.
a: Queues fit work that can wait: claim with SKIP LOCKED, retry on crash
A call can't wait and can't move: audio bound to one process, a frame every 20 ms
So the media server pushes the call to a worker with capacity, one process per call
Capacity is CPU per call: load-test calls per container, scale out with replicas
Cost: a crash drops that call, so drain workers on deploy instead of killing them

say: Work that can wait goes in a queue. A worker claims a row with SKIP LOCKED, and if it dies, another one picks it up. A call can't wait and can't move: its audio is bound to one process for minutes. So the media server dispatches it straight to a worker with room, and it runs in its own process. Capacity is CPU per call, so you scale by adding workers.
avoid: Saying a crashed call is retried like a job: the stream lives in that process

topics.title: The whole path, said in a minute
topics.brief: Put the pieces in order: signalling sets the call up, media flows separately, the media server makes the caller a participant, a room is created per call and an agent dispatched into it, and the agent reaches the backend through one authorization step. The nuance: the hop you stumble on when you say it aloud is the hop an interviewer will ask about.
points: Phone: carrier to SIP trunk to the media server's SIP service, one room per call
Web: the backend checks the login and issues a room token; the browser joins over WebRTC
Dispatch: room created, agent dispatched, the worker runs the call in its own process
Backend door: one authorize step says who is calling and returns a short-lived, scoped token
Name each hop's idea: signalling, media, room, dispatch, authorization
production: LiveKit inbound call workflow: identify the SIP caller from the participant's attributes, then let the agent answer
LiveKit SIP trunk setup: an inbound trunk accepts calls; a dispatch rule decides which room and agent each call gets
Scoped, short-lived tokens: the worker holds only what one call needs, and it expires

mcq.q: The media server has accepted an inbound SIP call. What happens next?
o: The agent publishes its greeting audio
The browser exchanges SDP with the SFU
The worker claims the call from a job queue
A dispatch rule creates a room and an agent is dispatched into it
The authorize step mints a room token for a browser
mcq.why: The dispatch rule maps the call to a room and an agent. The agent can only greet once it is in the room.

mcq.q: Why give the voice worker a short-lived, scoped token rather than a service key?
o: Service keys are too slow to verify
Scoped tokens lower audio latency
LiveKit refuses workers that hold service keys
It lets the worker send on the user's behalf without asking
If a call or the worker is compromised, the damage is limited to that call and expires
mcq.why: Least privilege per call: a leaked token does little and stops working soon. A service key would open everything.

open.q: What happens between the phone ringing and the agent speaking?
open.probe: Do you know what each piece is for, not only its name?
a: SIP over the trunk sets the call up; RTP carries the audio separately over UDP
The media server makes the caller a participant in a room, one room per call
A worker is dispatched into the room and runs the call in its own process
It authorizes first: who is calling, what they may do, a short-lived token
It subscribes to the caller's audio and publishes its greeting

say: Two things travel separately. SIP sets the call up through the trunk, and the audio comes as RTP packets over UDP. In alfred_ the call lands in LiveKit, one room per call, and a Python worker joins it as one more participant. Before it does anything it calls one authorize function with a short time budget, which says who is calling and hands back a short-lived, scoped token. Then it subscribes to the caller's audio and publishes its own.

topics.title: Audio as numbers, and what speech models read
topics.brief: Sound in a computer is a list of samples, and the sample rate caps the highest frequency at half the rate (Nyquist), so 8 kHz phone audio holds nothing above 4 kHz. Speech models rarely read raw samples: speech-to-text reads a log-mel spectrogram and writes text tokens, and text-to-speech runs the other way, ending in a vocoder. The nuance: a model trained on wideband audio loses detail it relied on when it hears a phone line.
points: Sample rate: samples per second; the highest frequency kept is half of it
Phone against web: 8 kHz keeps up to 4 kHz; web audio is 16 to 48 kHz
Frames: 10 to 20 ms chunks, the unit every downstream stage works on
Log-mel spectrogram: energy per frequency band over time, on a scale that matches hearing; what Whisper's encoder reads
Speech-to-text: encoder-decoder transformer, spectrogram in, text tokens out; streaming models emit words before the utterance ends
Text-to-speech: text to acoustic features or audio tokens, then a vocoder or codec decoder to a waveform; streaming TTS emits audio in chunks
production: Whisper: an encoder-decoder transformer trained on 680,000 hours of weakly supervised audio, reading 80-channel log-mel spectrograms
Phone paths: speech providers offer telephony-tuned models because 8 kHz mu-law audio differs from the wideband audio most models train on
Neural TTS: a front end normalises text, an acoustic model predicts features, a vocoder renders sound (Soniox's overview)

mcq.q: A speech model trained on 16 kHz audio does worse on phone calls. What is the main reason?
o: Phone audio is 8 kHz, so nothing above 4 kHz survives and detail the model learned on is gone
Phone audio arrives in larger frames the model cannot split
Phone calls are encrypted, which distorts the samples
Phone audio is stereo and the model expects mono
Phone calls have more background noise than any web call
mcq.why: Nyquist: the highest frequency kept is half the sample rate. The model's training audio had information the call does not.

mcq.q: What does a speech-to-text model like Whisper take as input?
o: The raw waveform, one sample per input token
Text tokens from a phonetic dictionary
The RTP packets as they arrive
A log-mel spectrogram: energy per frequency band over time
One feature vector for the whole utterance
mcq.why: The encoder reads a log-mel spectrogram; the decoder writes text tokens, like translating audio to text.

mcq.q: In text-to-speech, what turns the model's acoustic output into sound?
o: The spectrogram is played through the speaker as is
A vocoder or codec decoder that produces the waveform
The encoder of an encoder-decoder transformer
The voice activity detector
The jitter buffer on the receiving side
mcq.why: TTS predicts acoustic features or audio tokens first. A separate vocoder or decoder renders the waveform.

open.q: Our agent's transcripts are noticeably worse on phone calls than in the app. Why might that be, and what would you check?
open.probe: Whether you understand sample rate and what the model was trained on.
a: Phone audio is 8 kHz G.711, so nothing above 4 kHz and some compression loss
Models trained on wideband audio lose cues they rely on
Check per-channel error rates on real calls, not a blended number
Try a telephony-tuned model or one trained on 8 kHz input
Trade-off: a phone-specific model means two configurations to maintain and test

say: Phone audio is 8 kHz, so anything above 4 kHz is gone, and it's compressed on top. Most speech models are trained on wider-band audio, so they lose detail they rely on. The way I'd check it is to split error rates by phone and web on real calls. Then try a model tuned for telephony on the phone path.
avoid: Going into the maths of the spectrogram: the shape and where latency comes from are enough

topics.title: Knowing when the caller has finished
topics.brief: Two different questions. Voice activity detection asks whether there is speech in this frame; end-of-turn detection asks whether the caller has finished their thought. Silence alone is a bad signal because people pause mid-sentence, so you add a turn-detection model that reads the words. The nuance: the wait you pick is the whole feel of the agent, too short cuts people off, too long makes every reply slow.
points: VAD: is there speech in this frame; a small model such as Silero run on every frame
End of turn: have they finished; a separate decision from VAD
Endpointing: wait a set silence before ending the turn; simple, but pauses fool it
Turn-detection model: reads the words so far as well as the silence, so 'my number is' does not end a turn
The trade-off: short wait interrupts people, long wait makes every reply feel slow
Preemptive generation: start the reply before the turn is certain and throw it away if they keep talking
production: LiveKit turn detection: VAD, speech-to-text endpointing, a turn-detector model, realtime model detection, or manual control
LiveKit endpointing: a minimum and maximum delay, with the turn detector deciding where in that window to answer
Silero VAD: per its README, about 1 ms per 30 ms chunk on one CPU thread, cheap enough for every frame
Deepgram endpointing: the streaming service marks a final transcript after a set silence, configurable per request

mcq.q: What question does voice activity detection answer?
o: Has the caller finished their thought?
Which words were spoken?
Is there speech in this frame?
Who is speaking on the line?
Is the caller interrupting the agent?
mcq.why: VAD is per frame and knows nothing about meaning. Deciding the turn is over is a separate step.

mcq.q: Callers keep getting cut off when they pause to think mid-sentence. What is the best first change?
o: Lower the VAD threshold so it hears quieter speech
Shorten the silence needed before a turn ends
Switch the codec from G.711 to Opus
Make the jitter buffer larger
Use a turn-detection model that reads the words, not silence alone
mcq.why: The pause is real silence, so VAD is right and still ends the turn. Only something that reads the words can tell a thinking pause from an ending.

mcq.q: What does preemptive generation trade away to make replies faster?
o: Some wasted model calls, since a draft is discarded when the caller keeps talking
Transcript accuracy, in exchange for lower cost
A longer end-of-turn wait, in exchange for fewer interruptions
Audio quality, in exchange for bandwidth
Tool calls, in exchange for a smaller prompt
mcq.why: Starting before the turn is certain hides model time, at the cost of throwing some work away.

open.q: Elderly patients say our agent keeps talking over them. How would you fix it without making the agent feel slow for everyone else?
open.probe: VAD against end of turn, and treating the wait as a measured trade-off.
a: Separate the two decisions: VAD says speech, end of turn says done
Add a turn-detection model that reads the words, not silence alone
Widen the endpointing window rather than raising one fixed wait
Start generating preemptively so a longer wait costs less
Measure interruptions and time to first audio on recorded calls before and after

say: I'd first separate the two questions. VAD only says someone is speaking right now. Whether they're done is a different call, and silence alone gets it wrong because people pause mid-sentence. So I'd use a turn-detection model that reads the words, and start generating early so a slightly longer wait doesn't cost much. Then I'd measure interruptions and time to first audio on real calls, not guess.
avoid: Treating VAD and end-of-turn detection as the same thing

topics.title: Streaming every stage, and the latency budget
topics.brief: If each stage waited for the one before, a reply would take seconds. So every stage streams into the next: partial transcripts, streamed tokens, sentences chunked into speech while the model still writes. The number that matters is time to first audio, from the caller stopping to the agent's first sound, about 1 to 1.5 s as a design budget. The nuance: you settle latency arguments with per-stage timings on real turns, not with the budget.
points: Streaming: every stage feeds the next before the previous one finishes
Time to first audio: what the caller feels, not total reply time
Budget: end of turn 300 to 500 ms, final transcript 100 to 200, first token 300 to 500, first audio 100 to 200, network 100 to 150
Total: about 1 to 1.5 s; these are targets, not measurements
Critical path: keep the model there small; slow work, like a record lookup, runs while the agent says something natural
Measure per stage: log each stage per turn so you know which one grew
production: Deepgram: interim results stream while you speak; endpointing marks the final transcript
LiveKit turn tuning: endpointing delay and preemptive generation are the two main levers on time to first audio
Streaming TTS: synthesis starts on the first sentence, so first audio arrives while the rest is generated (Picovoice)
Parallel agents: a fast agent answers while a heavier one works the same request, so the caller hears something quickly

mcq.q: Which latency number does the caller actually feel?
o: Total time to generate the full reply
Model tokens per second
Transcript word error rate
Time from the caller stopping to the agent's first audio
Round-trip time of one RTP packet
mcq.why: Once the agent is speaking, the rest of the reply can arrive while it talks. The silence before the first sound is what feels slow.

mcq.q: Why start text-to-speech before the model has finished its answer?
o: TTS needs the full text to plan prosody, so it should start early
Speaking the first sentence while the rest is written takes generation time out of time to first audio
It lowers the cost of the model call
It lets the turn detector run faster
It removes the need for a jitter buffer
mcq.why: Streaming overlaps the stages. Without it, the whole generation time sits in front of the first sound.

mcq.q: Turns that used to take about 1 s to first audio now take 2.5 s. What do you do first?
o: Switch to a realtime speech-to-speech model
Shorten the end-of-turn wait
Look at per-stage timings for those turns to find which stage grew
Add more worker containers
Cut the system prompt in half
mcq.why: Every other option is a guess about which stage is slow. Per-stage timings tell you.

open.q: Walk me through one turn of a voice call, and where the time goes.
open.probe: Real-time depth: streaming, the metric that matters, and measuring instead of guessing.
a: End of turn decides they're done: 300 to 500 ms, the number that makes it feel conversational
Final transcript 100 to 200 ms; first model token 300 to 500
Streaming TTS gives first audio in 100 to 200 ms; the phone line adds 100 to 150
About 1 to 1.5 s to first audio; a slow lookup gets a natural filler, not dead air
These are targets; log every stage per turn so the argument is settled with data

say: The caller stops, and end-of-turn detection decides they're done, about 300 to 500 ms. The transcript is final about 100 to 200 ms later, a small model starts answering in 300 to 500, and streaming speech gives first audio 100 to 200 after that, plus the phone line. So about 1 to 1.5 seconds to first audio. In alfred_ a lean agent answers on the call while the main agent works the same request in parallel, so the caller hears something fast and the heavy work still happens. And my scenario harness gates on time to first audio, so I'm not guessing.

What's hard is that every stage adds up, so everything streams and the model on the critical path stays small. On MockFlow-AI, a voice interview platform I built on LiveKit, streaming every stage is how it runs under 400 ms end to end.
avoid: Quoting one latency number without saying where it starts and stops

topics.title: Interruptions, backchannels and silence
topics.brief: People talk over agents. On a barge-in the agent must stop its audio within a couple of hundred milliseconds, cancel what it was about to say, and listen. But 'mm-hm' is a backchannel that means keep going, and a cough is noise. The nuance: anything that must happen every time, like a filler during a slow lookup or a check-in on a quiet line, belongs in a timer in code, not in the prompt.
points: Barge-in: stop audio fast, cancel the pending reply, listen
Backchannel: 'mm-hm' means keep talking; a minimum speech duration filters it out
False interruption: a cough or a door; resume where you were
Echo cancellation: the agent's own voice coming back through the handset must not interrupt it
Silence rules: a filler when a lookup runs long, a check-in when the line goes quiet, a graceful hangup later
Code, not prompt: timers fire every time; a prompted filler only usually happens
production: LiveKit adaptive interruption handling: tells real interruptions from backchannels instead of stopping on any sound
OpenAI Realtime: on interruption the server truncates the assistant's audio item so the transcript matches what the caller heard
Cancellation as a pattern: barge-in is a priority cancel of in-flight work, the same idea as the guide's priority and cancellation technique

mcq.q: A caller says 'mm-hm' while the agent explains how to prepare for a procedure. What should the agent do?
o: Stop and listen, since any speech is a barge-in
Stop, apologise and repeat the sentence
End the TTS stream and start a new turn
Ask the caller to repeat themselves
Keep talking: it is a backchannel
mcq.why: A backchannel says 'I'm listening, go on'. Stopping for it makes the agent jumpy.

mcq.q: The caller says 'wait, no, Thursday' over the agent. What must happen?
o: Stop audio within a couple of hundred ms, cancel the pending reply, and listen
Finish the current sentence, then listen
Lower the volume and keep going
Queue the caller's words for after the reply
Restart the turn from the greeting
mcq.why: That is real speech changing the request. Anything already generated is now wrong and must be cancelled.

mcq.q: A lookup takes 3 s. Why put the 'let me check' filler on a timer in code rather than in the prompt?
o: Code fillers sound more natural than model speech
The model cannot produce short phrases
Timers cut the model's token cost to zero
It must happen every time, and a prompt only makes it likely
Prompts cannot mention tools
mcq.why: A model follows instructions most of the time. Behaviour that must never be skipped belongs in deterministic code.

open.q: A patient interrupts the agent halfway through reading their appointment details. What should happen, and how do you avoid stopping for every 'okay'?
open.probe: Barge-in as cancellation, and the line between interruption and backchannel.
a: Real speech: stop audio fast, cancel the pending reply, listen
Truncate what the agent said so the history matches what the caller heard
Backchannels and short noises: a minimum speech duration, keep going or resume
Echo cancellation so the agent never interrupts itself
Test it: barge-in and false interruptions as scenarios, not anecdotes

say: If it's real speech, the agent stops talking within a couple of hundred milliseconds, cancels what it was about to say, and listens. If it's 'okay' or 'mm-hm', that's the caller saying keep going, so a minimum speech duration filters it out, and after a cough it resumes. Fillers and check-ins I'd put on timers in code, because they have to happen every time. My scenario harness has a gate on barge-in and on dead air for exactly this.
avoid: Saying the agent should stop on any sound: that makes it jumpy

topics.title: Realtime speech-to-speech or a cascade
topics.brief: A cascade is three models in a row, speech-to-text, a text model, text-to-speech, so you control each stage, get a transcript at every step and can put your own turn detection in front. A realtime speech-to-speech model takes audio in and gives audio out: lower latency and more natural prosody, but tool calling and transcripts come on the provider's terms. The nuance: keep both behind one seam and let evals pick, because the answer changes with each model release.
points: Cascade: control, a transcript at every step, any text model, your own turn detection
Realtime: lower latency and natural speech, less control
One seam: both arms behind one interface, picked per call from config
Evals decide: the same scenarios on both arms, gated on quality and time to first audio
Config risk: on some providers the realtime session config is all or nothing, so one unsupported option can silently drop turn detection
Allowlist: keep a measured list of supported realtime options per model version
production: OpenAI Realtime: speech to speech over WebRTC or WebSocket, with server-side turn detection
Pipecat: a cascade framework where you place your own VAD and turn detection in front of speech-to-text
LiveKit Agents: supports both a realtime model and a speech-to-text, LLM, TTS pipeline behind the same agent session

mcq.q: When would you choose a cascade over a realtime speech-to-speech model?
o: When latency matters more than anything else
When you need your own turn detection, a specific text model and a transcript at every step
When you want the most natural prosody
When you want fewer moving parts
When you want the provider to own tool calling
mcq.why: A cascade buys control and visibility at each stage, at the cost of some latency and naturalness.

mcq.q: A realtime voice session worked in testing, then turn detection silently stopped after a config change. What is the likely cause?
o: The VAD model ran out of memory
The SIP trunk changed codec
An unsupported option made the provider drop the whole session config
The jitter buffer grew too large
The model's context window filled up
mcq.why: Some providers reject a session update as a whole. One bad field and the turn detection settings go with it, with no loud error.

mcq.q: You have a realtime arm and a cascade arm behind one seam. How should you decide which ships?
o: Pick the one with the lower list price
Ship the newest model
Ask a few people which sounds better
Pick realtime, because it has lower latency
Run both through the same eval scenarios and let the measured results decide
mcq.why: Latency, task success and audio quality trade against each other, and change with every release. A gate on the same scenarios makes it a measured choice.

open.q: Would you build our scheduling agent on a realtime speech-to-speech model or a cascade? Defend it.
open.probe: Trade-off reasoning, and whether you'd let measurement decide.
a: Realtime: lower latency, natural speech; cascade: control, transcripts, own turn detection
Scheduling needs reliable tool calls and an audit trail of what was heard
Keep both behind one seam, picked per call from config
Run the same scenarios on both, gated on task success and time to first audio
Watch config risk: an all-or-nothing session update can drop turn detection silently

say: I wouldn't pick one up front. Realtime gives lower latency and more natural speech; a cascade gives control, a transcript at every step, and my own turn detection. For scheduling, reliable tool calls and a clear record of what was heard matter a lot. So I'd keep both behind one seam, run the same scenarios on both, and let the gates on task success and time to first audio decide.

topics.title: Edge functions against long-running workers
topics.brief: An edge function is a short-lived invocation: a request comes in, an isolate handles it within a time and memory limit, and it scales to zero. A long-running worker is a process you keep alive: it can hold a call for minutes, keep models warm and keep connections open. The nuance: the rule is about lifetime and state, not speed; if the work outlives a request or needs warm state, it needs a worker.
points: Process and container: a running program with its own memory; a container packages a process with its files
Edge function: short, stateless, time-limited, scales to zero; ideal for request and response
Worker: long-lived, holds state and connections, and you pay for it while idle
Rule of thumb: shorter than the request and stateless, use a function; outlives the request or needs warm state, use a worker
Voice: the authorization check fits a function; the agent holding the call needs a worker
production: Supabase Edge Functions: 2 s of CPU time per request, a 150 to 400 s wall clock, and 256 MB of memory
Railway services: either a long-running container or a scheduled job, the choice this topic is about
LiveKit server lifecycle: a worker advertises its capacity for load balancing and drains live calls on deploy

mcq.q: Why can't the voice agent itself run as an edge function?
o: Edge functions cannot make outbound network calls
A call lasts minutes and needs warm models and an open media connection, beyond a function's limits
Edge functions cannot read environment variables
Edge functions always respond more slowly than containers
LiveKit cannot dispatch to anything but a container
mcq.why: Functions are bounded in wall clock, CPU and memory and are torn down after the request. A call is long and stateful.

mcq.q: Which job fits an edge function best?
o: Holding a WebSocket to a speech model for a whole call
Keeping a voice activity model warm in memory
Running a 20-minute batch transcription
A quick authorization check that returns a scoped token
Consuming a queue continuously
mcq.why: Short, stateless request and response is what functions do well. The others outlive a request or need warm state.

mcq.q: What does a long-running worker cost you that an edge function does not?
o: You pay for it while it sits idle
It cannot keep state between requests
It must finish within 2 s of CPU
It cannot scale past one instance
It cannot open outbound connections
mcq.why: A function scales to zero between requests. A worker stays up, which is the point and the cost.

open.q: Draw where each piece of a voice agent runs. Why is the agent a container and not a serverless function?
open.probe: Whether you choose infrastructure by lifetime and state, with reasons.
a: Edge function: short, stateless, time-limited, scales to zero
Worker: holds a call for minutes, warm models, open connections
Auth check as a function; the agent as a worker
Trade-off: workers cost money idle and need drain on deploy
Example: Supabase functions cap CPU at 2 s and memory at 256 MB, so a call can't live there

say: The way I decide is lifetime and state. If the work is shorter than the request and holds no state, it's a function. A call lasts minutes and needs warm models and an open media connection, so it's a long-running worker. In alfred_ the voice agent is a Python worker, and its only door to the backend is an authorize function with a short time budget. That split is pretty much the rule in practice.
avoid: Saying functions are slow: the limit is lifetime and state, not speed

topics.title: Push and pull, and at-least-once
topics.brief: Pull: jobs sit in a queue and workers claim them; in Postgres, SKIP LOCKED lets many workers grab different rows without waiting, and a lease with a heartbeat turns a crash into a retry. Push: a dispatcher hands work to a worker it chose, as LiveKit does with calls. The nuance: leases give at-least-once delivery, so a job can run twice, and every effect it has must be safe to repeat.
points: SKIP LOCKED: each worker skips rows others hold, so no two take the same job and none wait
Lease: claimed_at plus a timeout; a heartbeat extends it while the worker is alive
At-least-once: a job may run twice, never zero times; effects must be idempotent
Push: a dispatcher picks the worker; fits live sessions that can't wait
Pull: workers pick the work; fits jobs that can wait, retry and survive a crash
production: Postgres: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in the locking clause, the basis of most Postgres-backed job queues
AWS SQS standard queues: at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent
Kleppmann: a lease alone is unsafe after a long pause; fencing tokens stop a stale worker from writing
Crunchy Data: message queuing in native Postgres, without a separate broker

mcq.q: What does SKIP LOCKED add over a plain SELECT ... FOR UPDATE?
o: It deletes the row once a worker claims it
It locks the whole table so only one worker runs
Workers skip rows others have locked instead of waiting, so they claim different jobs in parallel
It guarantees each job runs exactly once
It retries a failed job automatically
mcq.why: Plain FOR UPDATE makes the second worker wait on the first. SKIP LOCKED moves it on to the next free row.

mcq.q: A worker sends a reminder SMS, then crashes before marking the job done. With leases, what happens?
o: The job is lost because the worker held the lock
The database rolls back the SMS
The job stays locked forever
The queue marks it done because the send succeeded
The lease expires, another worker claims the job, and the SMS goes again unless the send is idempotent
mcq.why: The queue only knows the job was not marked done. It retries, and the effect repeats unless it is keyed.

mcq.q: Which delivery guarantee does a lease-based queue give you?
o: Exactly once, because the row is locked
At least once: a job may run twice, never zero times
At most once: a crashed job is dropped
Exactly once, if heartbeats are frequent enough
Strict order, one job at a time
mcq.why: A crash after the effect and before the commit means a rerun. Exactly once has to be built on top with idempotency.

open.q: Our reminder calls and SMS run from a job queue. A worker dies halfway through. What happens, and how do you keep a patient from getting two reminders?
open.probe: Leases, at-least-once delivery, and making effects safe to repeat.
a: Workers claim rows with SKIP LOCKED under a lease with a heartbeat
The dead worker's lease expires; another claims the job
That is at-least-once: the job can run twice
So the send is idempotent: a key per reminder, stored with the result
Contrast: live calls are pushed to a worker, not queued, because they can't wait

say: Workers claim jobs with SKIP LOCKED, under a lease with a heartbeat. If one dies, the lease runs out and another worker picks the job up. That means a job can run twice, so whatever it does has to be safe to repeat. I'd key each reminder so a second run finds the first result and stops. Calls are different: they're pushed straight to a worker, because they can't wait in a queue.
avoid: Claiming a queue gives exactly-once delivery

topics.title: Idempotency: a retry must not do it twice
topics.brief: Retries happen because you can't tell a lost request from a lost response: the booking may exist and only the reply timed out. An idempotency key makes the retry safe: the client sends the same key every attempt, the server stores key and result in the same transaction as the effect, and a repeat returns the stored result. The nuance: if the key and the effect are written separately, a crash between them brings back the double booking.
points: Lost request or lost response: a timeout can't tell you which, so you retry
Same key: the client sends one key on every attempt of one action
Same transaction: key, result and effect commit together
Repeat: a request with a known key returns the stored result and does nothing new
Layers: tool calls, drafts and sends, and session setup can each be keyed
Confirm before acting: a write the caller cares about is drafted, then confirmed, then executed once
production: Stripe: clients send an Idempotency-Key header; the first result, success or error, is saved and replayed for repeats, and keys expire after 24 hours
Brandur Leach: Stripe-like keys in Postgres, with recovery points so a request interrupted halfway can resume
Agent tools: an execution layer keys each write so a retried tool call replays the stored result instead of acting twice

mcq.q: A booking request to the EHR times out. What do you know?
o: Nothing certain: the booking may have been made and only the reply lost
The booking failed, so it is safe to resend without a key
The booking succeeded, so do not retry
The EHR is down and all calls should stop
The idempotency key has expired
mcq.why: A timeout means no answer, not a no. That uncertainty is why retries need a key.

mcq.q: Why must the idempotency key be stored in the same transaction as the effect?
o: It makes the key lookup faster
Keys must be encrypted together with the effect
Postgres cannot index keys outside a transaction
A crash between separate writes leaves an effect with no key, so the retry does it again
It lets two different requests share one key
mcq.why: Atomicity is the whole guarantee. Either the effect and its key both exist, or neither does.

mcq.q: A retry arrives with the same key as a booking that already succeeded. What should the server return?
o: An error saying the key was already used
A new booking with a new confirmation number
The stored result of the first attempt, without booking again
A 202 telling the client to poll later
Nothing, and drop the request silently
mcq.why: The client needs the answer it missed. Returning the stored result gives it that without a second effect.

open.q: How does a retried booking avoid booking twice?
open.probe: The write-back safety every voice agent needs, and where the transaction boundary goes.
a: A timeout can't tell a lost request from a lost response, so you retry
The client sends the same idempotency key on every attempt
The server stores key and result in the same transaction as the booking
A repeat with that key returns the stored result and books nothing
Against an EHR that has no keys: record intent first, then check for the booking before retrying

say: You can't tell a lost request from a lost response, so you retry. The client sends the same idempotency key on every attempt, and the server stores the key and the result in the same transaction as the booking. A repeat with that key gets the stored result back and nothing is booked again. In alfred_ tools go through an execution layer with idempotency on writes, so a retried action replays instead of acting twice, and sends are drafted, then confirmed by the person. For an EHR booking I'd apply the same idea, and check how the EHR itself handles retries.

topics.title: Timeouts, budgets and retries
topics.brief: Every network call needs a timeout, and each one must fit inside its caller's budget, or the outer layer gives up before the inner one reports. When something fails you retry with exponential backoff and jitter, so clients that failed together don't retry together. The nuance: whether to fail open or closed when a check can't run is a product decision, and it should be written in code.
points: Timeout: every network call has one; no call waits forever
Nested budgets: an inner timeout is shorter than its caller's, so the inner step fails and reports first
Backoff with jitter: spreads retries out so they don't arrive as one wave
Retry storms: retries arrive exactly when the service has least capacity
Fail closed: when the answer is no, deny
Fail open: when the checker itself is down, allow, if the risk of letting a call through is lower than dropping every call
production: AWS Builders' Library: capped exponential backoff with jitter, and retrying at one layer only so retries don't multiply up the stack
Circuit breakers: stop calling a dependency that keeps failing and fail fast until it recovers
Short auth budgets: a voice worker's authorize call gets a few seconds at most, since the caller is waiting on the line

mcq.q: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
o: To make each retry faster than the last
To cap the number of retries
To skip retries for calls that are not idempotent
To keep timeouts inside the caller's budget
So clients that failed together do not retry together in one wave
mcq.why: Backoff alone keeps synchronised clients synchronised. Randomness spreads them out.

mcq.q: The service the authorization step depends on is unreachable. When is failing open acceptable?
o: Always, because availability beats correctness
When letting a call through is less risky than dropping every call, and that choice is written down
Never, because security checks must always fail closed
Only when the caller has called before
Only after one round of retries has failed
mcq.why: It depends on what an unchecked call can do. A scoped, short-lived token can make failing open on a down checker a reasonable choice; a definite no still fails closed.

mcq.q: A handler has a 5 s budget, and its caller waits 8 s for it. Why that order?
o: A longer outer timeout makes the inner call faster
The outer timeout should always equal the inner one
The inner step should keep retrying until the outer one expires
Each inner timeout fits inside its caller's, so the inner step fails and reports before the outer one gives up
The order does not matter as long as both exist
mcq.why: If the outer layer gives up first, it can't tell a slow success from a failure, and may retry work that completed.

open.q: Mid-call, the agent's lookup against the scheduling system starts timing out. What should the system do?
open.probe: Timeouts that fit a budget, safe retries, and failing deliberately.
a: A timeout on the call that fits the turn's budget, with a filler so the line isn't silent
Retry with backoff and jitter, only if the call is idempotent
If it keeps failing, a circuit breaker stops hammering the system
Decide the failure mode: offer a callback or a human rather than guess
Write the fail-open or fail-closed choice in code, and alert on it

say: Every call gets a timeout that fits inside the turn's budget, and the agent says something natural while it waits. I'd retry with backoff and jitter, but only if the call is safe to repeat. If it keeps failing, stop hammering it and offer the patient a callback or a person, rather than guess. In alfred_ the worker's authorize call has a short time budget for the same reason: the caller is waiting on the line.

Peak and burst: size for the burst, not the daily average

Scale out: replicas, with the dispatcher sending each new call to a worker with room

modules.blurb: Explain and write the asyncio that holds live calls: the loop, tasks, queues, cancellation for barge-in, and what never to do on the loop.

topics.title: One thread, many calls
topics.brief: asyncio runs many tasks on one thread. A task runs until it awaits something that is not ready, then the event loop runs another task that is. Nothing runs in parallel: one process holds several calls because most of a call is waiting, and the waits overlap.
points: Coroutine: calling an async def function makes a coroutine object and runs nothing until it is awaited or wrapped in a task
Task: asyncio.create_task schedules a coroutine to run alongside the current one; awaiting the task collects its result
Await: the only place a task gives up the thread, so code between two awaits runs without interruption
I/O bound: async pays off when work is mostly waiting (audio frames, model tokens, tool replies); CPU work gains nothing from it
Weak references: the loop keeps only weak references to tasks, so keep your own reference or a fire-and-forget task can be garbage collected mid-flight
production: livekit-agents, a common framework for Python voice workers, is built on asyncio: a call's audio, model stream and tool calls are tasks on one loop
FastAPI runs async def endpoints on the event loop and plain def endpoints in a threadpool (AnyIO's default limit is 40 threads)
uvicorn can run on uvloop, a faster drop-in event loop built on libuv; the programming model stays the same

mcq.q: A worker holds eight calls in one asyncio process on one thread. What lets it serve all eight?
o: The loop runs each coroutine on its own CPU core, in parallel
asyncio preempts each task every few milliseconds, like an OS scheduler
Each call mostly awaits I/O, and the loop runs another ready task at every await
The GIL is released inside async def functions, so coroutines run side by side
Each create_task call starts a hidden thread that the loop supervises
mcq.why: asyncio is cooperative: tasks switch only at await. It works because the waits of different calls overlap, not because anything runs at the same time.

mcq.q: You call fetch_slots(), an async def function, without await and without create_task. What happens?
o: It runs in the background and its result is discarded
A coroutine object is made, nothing runs, and Python warns it was never awaited
It runs synchronously and blocks until it returns
It is scheduled on the loop and starts at the next await
It raises TypeError at once because async functions need await
mcq.why: Calling a coroutine function only builds the coroutine. It runs when awaited or wrapped in a task; otherwise you get 'coroutine was never awaited'.

mcq.q: Why is `if key not in pending: pending[key] = fut` safe in asyncio without a lock, but unsafe once an await sits between the check and the set?
o: Dict operations are atomic in CPython, so the await makes no difference
asyncio wraps each dict access in an internal lock that await releases
Tasks run in creation order, so the first task always reaches the set first
Tasks switch only at await, so with none in between no other task can run there
Each coroutine works on a copy of shared state until it awaits
mcq.why: Between two awaits a task cannot be interrupted by another task. Put an await between check and set and a second task can pass the same check.

open.q: Our worker runs several live calls in one Python process. Walk me through how that works, and what can go wrong.
open.probe: Whether he understands cooperative scheduling and its one big failure mode.
a: One thread, one event loop; every call is a set of tasks
A task runs until it awaits something not ready; the loop then runs another ready task
It works because a call is mostly waiting: audio frames, tokens, tool replies
What goes wrong: anything that does not await (a sync library, CPU work) freezes every call on that process
So I/O uses async clients, CPU work goes to a thread or process, and I watch loop lag

say: I think the key word is cooperative. Everything runs on one thread, and tasks only take turns at an await.
It works for calls because a call is mostly waiting, on audio, on the model, on a tool, so the waits overlap.
The worker in the voice agent I own is Python on livekit-agents, so this is the model I work in every day.
The flip side is one blocking call stalls every call on that process, so that is the first thing I look for.
avoid: Saying asyncio runs calls in parallel: it is concurrency on one thread, and they will probe the difference

topics.title: Gather, TaskGroup and queues
topics.brief: gather and TaskGroup both run awaitables together and wait for them. The difference people miss is failure: gather leaves the other tasks running when one fails, TaskGroup cancels them. Between pipeline stages a bounded asyncio.Queue gives backpressure, but a live phone stream cannot be slowed, so real-time stages drop old frames instead of blocking the reader.
points: asyncio.gather: runs awaitables together and returns results in order; the first exception reaches the awaiter, but the other tasks are not cancelled
return_exceptions=True: gather returns exceptions as results instead of raising, so one failure does not hide the others
TaskGroup (3.11+): an async with block; if one task fails the rest are cancelled, and errors come out as an ExceptionGroup, handled with except*
asyncio.Queue(maxsize=n): put waits when full and get waits when empty; that wait is the backpressure
Real-time source: a microphone or phone stream cannot wait, so a full queue there means drop the oldest frames or shed load, never stall the reader
production: The Python docs' worker pool: N consumer tasks on one asyncio.Queue, with queue.join() waiting until every item is marked task_done()
Fan-out inside a turn: calendar and contacts lookups under one TaskGroup, so when one fails the sibling is cancelled instead of left running
Live media uses bounded buffers with a drop policy: a WebRTC jitter buffer holds tens of milliseconds of audio and discards late packets rather than growing

mcq.q: A turn fetches calendar and contacts with asyncio.gather and default arguments. The contacts call raises. What happens to the calendar call?
o: It is cancelled at once, and gather raises the contacts error
It is cancelled, and both errors come out as an ExceptionGroup
gather waits for it to finish, then raises the contacts error
It keeps running; gather raises the contacts error but does not cancel it
gather returns the calendar result and None for contacts
mcq.why: With default arguments gather propagates the first exception to the awaiter and leaves the other awaitables running. Cancelling siblings is what TaskGroup adds.

mcq.q: Same turn inside `async with asyncio.TaskGroup()`. The contacts task raises ValueError. What do you get?
o: The calendar task finishes, then the block raises the bare ValueError
The calendar task is cancelled, and the block raises an ExceptionGroup holding the ValueError
The calendar task keeps running after the block exits
The block exits normally and the error is only logged
The calendar task is cancelled, and the bare ValueError is raised
mcq.why: TaskGroup cancels the remaining tasks when one fails and raises an ExceptionGroup, which you handle with except* ValueError.

mcq.q: Speech to text falls behind the stage feeding it audio. The queue between them has no maxsize. What happens?
o: put() starts waiting once the consumer lags, slowing the producer
asyncio drops the oldest frames when memory runs low
The queue raises QueueFull and the producer task crashes
The loop gives the slow consumer extra turns until it catches up
Frames pile up, the transcript lags further behind, and memory grows without limit
mcq.why: An unbounded queue never pushes back. Overload shows up late, as lag and then memory exhaustion, instead of early, as a waiting producer.

mcq.q: A bounded queue is fed by a live phone stream and fills up. Which policy fits?
o: Drop the oldest frames, or shed the call, so the stream reader never stalls
await put() so the phone stream slows to match the consumer
Raise maxsize until the queue never fills in testing
Move the queue into a thread so it can grow without blocking
Use put_nowait and let QueueFull end the call
mcq.why: Backpressure only works when the producer can wait. A caller keeps talking regardless, so stale audio is dropped and fresh audio kept.

open.q: You have audio in, transcription, the model and speech out in one process. How do you connect them, and what happens when one stage falls behind?
open.probe: Whether he knows backpressure, and where it does not apply.
a: Each stage is a task; stages are joined by asyncio.Queue or async streams
Bounded queues, so a slow stage makes the one before it wait instead of hiding the overload
At the live edge nothing can wait: drop the oldest audio or shed the call
Run the stages under one TaskGroup, so one failing stage cancels the rest of that call
Watch queue depth per stage: a growing queue names the slow stage

say: The way I'd do it, each stage is a task and a bounded queue sits between them, so a slow stage pushes back instead of quietly piling up.
The exception is the edge where audio comes in. A caller doesn't slow down because we're behind, so there I'd drop old frames.
And I'd put one call's stages in a TaskGroup, so if one dies the rest go with it. Pretty much, fail the whole call cleanly, not half of it.
avoid: Saying gather cancels the other tasks on failure: that is TaskGroup

topics.title: Timeouts, cancellation and barge-in
topics.brief: task.cancel() asks a task to stop: CancelledError is raised inside it at the await where it is suspended, so it can clean up in finally. Barge-in is exactly this: the caller speaks, the speaking task is cancelled. The trap is a timeout that cancels work you meant to keep: a filler needs a wait that does not cancel the tool.
points: task.cancel(): a request, not a kill; CancelledError is raised at the await where the task is suspended, and a task busy in CPU code stops only when it next awaits
CancelledError: a BaseException since 3.8, so except Exception does not catch it; clean up in finally, and re-raise if you do catch it
asyncio.timeout(5): a context manager (3.11+) that cancels the block when it runs over and raises TimeoutError; wait_for does the same for one awaitable
asyncio.wait(timeout=...): returns done and pending sets and cancels nothing, which is what a filler needs
shield: protects the inner awaitable when the outer await is cancelled; the waiter stops, the work goes on
production: Filler pattern: start the tool as a task, asyncio.wait on it for 1.2 s, speak 'Let me check' if it is still pending, then keep awaiting the same task under a 5 s total timeout
LiveKit's agent framework treats interruption as a session setting: when the caller talks over the agent, playback stops and the agent listens
A cancelled write may already have reached the server, so a booking cut off by a timeout is retried with the same idempotency key, never assumed to have failed
TaskGroup and asyncio.timeout both depend on CancelledError propagating; Python 3.11 added Task.uncancel() for this bookkeeping, and swallowing the error breaks both

mcq.q: The caller interrupts. You call speak_task.cancel() while it is awaiting the next audio chunk. What happens?
o: The task stops instantly mid-word, and its finally block is skipped
The task finishes the current sentence, then exits normally
CancelledError is raised at that await on the next loop turn, so finally can stop the audio
cancel() blocks the caller until the task has fully stopped
TimeoutError is raised inside the task for the speaker to handle
mcq.why: cancel() schedules CancelledError into the task at the await where it waits. It returns at once, and the task cleans up in finally on its next turn.

mcq.q: You want 'Let me check' if a tool takes over 1.2 s, and then the tool's result. Which approach does that?
o: await asyncio.wait_for(task, 1.2), speak the filler on TimeoutError, then await task again
asyncio.wait({task}, timeout=1.2), speak the filler if it is pending, then await the same task
async with asyncio.timeout(1.2): await task, and retry the tool after the filler
Cancel the task after 1.2 s, speak the filler, then start a new task
await asyncio.sleep(1.2) before starting the tool, then speak and await it
mcq.why: wait_for and asyncio.timeout cancel the task when time runs out, so the tool dies. asyncio.wait only reports what is done and cancels nothing.

mcq.q: Your speaking coroutine wraps its body in `except Exception: log()`. Barge-in cancels it. What happens?
o: The handler catches CancelledError and the task keeps speaking
The handler logs it, and the task exits as cancelled
Python raises RuntimeError because the task swallowed a cancel
The handler does not run, since CancelledError is a BaseException; finally still runs
The cancel waits until the except block finishes
mcq.why: Since Python 3.8 CancelledError derives from BaseException, so broad except Exception handlers no longer swallow cancellation by accident.

mcq.q: A tool call that books a slot is cut off by its 5 s timeout. What should the agent assume?
o: It failed, so tell the caller and offer to try again
It succeeded, because the request left before the timeout
asyncio rolled back the HTTP request when it cancelled the task
Nothing reached the server, since cancellation stops the socket write
It may or may not have booked: retry with the same idempotency key, or check first
mcq.why: Cancellation stops your waiting, not the server. The outcome is unknown, so the safe moves are an idempotent retry or a read before speaking.

open.q: How would you implement barge-in and a 'let me check' filler in an asyncio voice worker?
open.probe: Whether he can turn cancellation semantics into correct call behaviour.
a: Speaking is its own task; when voice activity says the caller is talking, cancel it
Its finally block stops playback and records what was actually said
A tool call is a task; asyncio.wait for 1.2 s, filler if pending, then keep awaiting under a total timeout
Never wait_for the tool with the filler delay: that cancels the tool
A write cut off by a timeout has an unknown outcome: retry idempotently or check before speaking

say: Barge-in is cancellation. The agent speaking is a task, and when the caller starts talking I cancel it and stop the audio in a finally.
For the filler I race a timer against the tool, but with asyncio.wait, not wait_for, because wait_for would kill the tool at 1.2 seconds.
And if a write times out I don't know whether it happened. In the agent I own, writes go through idempotency, so a retry replays instead of acting twice.
avoid: Saying cancel() kills the task immediately: it raises at the next await, and CPU-bound code cannot be interrupted

topics.title: Never block the loop
topics.brief: Everything on the loop shares one thread, so one synchronous call freezes every call on that process, not only its own. It hides in testing because one call at a time feels fine. The fix depends on the work: async clients for I/O, a thread for blocking libraries, a process for pure-Python CPU work, because the GIL still applies inside threads.
points: Blocking call: requests.get, time.sleep, a sync database driver or a large file read inside async def holds the thread until it returns
asyncio.to_thread (3.9+): runs a blocking function in the default thread pool and awaits it; right for blocking I/O and C code that releases the GIL
Process pool: loop.run_in_executor with a ProcessPoolExecutor for pure-Python CPU work, which threads would still serialize on the GIL
Debug mode: asyncio.run(debug=True) or PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 logs any callback slower than 100 ms (loop.slow_callback_duration)
Symptom: stutter, late fillers and timeouts on every call at once, not on one
production: Async clients: httpx.AsyncClient or aiohttp instead of requests, asyncpg instead of a sync Postgres driver
FastAPI: a sync library is safe in a plain def endpoint (threadpool) and blocks the loop inside async def
Prewarming: load models such as voice activity detection at process start, not on the first call; livekit-agents offers a prewarm hook for this
The default thread pool has min(32, cpu_count + 4) workers since Python 3.8, so a burst of to_thread calls queues behind it

mcq.q: A coroutine calls requests.get() for a 2 s lookup. Four other calls are live on the process. What do they experience?
o: All four freeze for those 2 s: no audio frames, no tokens, no timers
Nothing, because the loop switches tasks while requests waits on the socket
Nothing, because the GIL is released during network I/O
A slight slowdown while the loop shares time with the request
asyncio detects the blocking call and moves it to a thread
mcq.why: requests releases the GIL for other threads, but the loop is one thread and it is stuck inside requests. No other task can run until it returns.

mcq.q: Voice activity detection written in pure Python takes 30 ms a frame and stalls the loop. Which fix lets it run truly in parallel with the loop?
o: Make it async def so the loop can switch away from it
Add await asyncio.sleep(0) after every frame
Run it with asyncio.to_thread so it runs alongside the loop
Raise loop.slow_callback_duration so it stops being flagged
Run it in a ProcessPoolExecutor through run_in_executor
mcq.why: Pure-Python CPU work in a thread still contends for the GIL with the loop. A separate process has its own interpreter and runs in parallel.

mcq.q: Resampling with numpy stalls the loop for 20 ms a frame. Why is asyncio.to_thread a reasonable fix here?
o: to_thread runs the function in a separate process
numpy releases the GIL in its C loops, so the thread works while the loop serves tasks
numpy calls become async once they run in a thread
Python threads always run truly in parallel
to_thread slices the work into 100 ms chunks for the loop
mcq.why: Threads help CPU work only when that work releases the GIL, as numpy and many audio and inference libraries do in native code.

open.q: A requests.get() inside a coroutine passed every test. Why is it a production bug, and how would you find others like it?
open.probe: Whether he connects one blocking call to every call on the process, and knows the tooling.
a: It is synchronous, so the loop thread waits inside it and every task on the process stops
Tests run one call at a time, so nobody else is waiting to notice
Fix: an async client, or asyncio.to_thread if the library has no async version
Find others: debug mode logs callbacks over 100 ms; measure loop lag under several concurrent test calls
CPU-heavy work (resampling, detection) goes to a thread if it releases the GIL, a process if not

say: It works in testing because only one call is running. In production that one call freezes every other call on the process for as long as the request takes.
I'd swap in an async client, or push it to a thread if there isn't one.
To find the rest I'd turn on asyncio debug mode, which flags anything over 100 milliseconds, and load the worker with several calls at once. One blocking line is enough to hurt everyone.
avoid: Saying to_thread fixes any CPU work: pure-Python CPU work still fights the GIL

topics.title: Build it: a small call orchestrator
topics.brief: The practical round may have you build a small backend live. The orchestrator puts the earlier topics together: a queue from a fake caller, one agent loop, a speaking task that new speech cancels, tool calls with a filler and a timeout, and a keyed send a retry cannot repeat. The nuance is a decision you state out loud: what happens to a running tool when the caller talks over it.
points: Shape: a fake caller puts utterances on an asyncio.Queue; one agent loop task takes them and decides
Speaking: a task that emits words with small sleeps; new speech cancels it and finally stops the audio
Tool call: create_task, wait 1.2 s, filler if pending, then await under a 5 s total timeout
Keyed send: put the future in a dict under the draft id before awaiting, so a concurrent retry awaits the same result instead of sending again
Interrupt policy: speaking is always cancelled; a read can keep running; a write never goes ahead without a fresh yes
Timestamps: log time.monotonic() on every event, so latency is read, not guessed
production: FastAPI WebSockets: one async endpoint per connection, with receive and send as separate tasks so a slow send never stops reads
websockets keepalive: the library pings every 20 s by default and closes the connection if no pong arrives within 20 s, which is how a dead peer is noticed
Idempotency keys as payment APIs use them: the server stores the first result under the key and returns it for any retry
time.monotonic() for latency, never time.time(), which can jump when the system clock is adjusted

mcq.q: Your send writes the result under the draft id only after `await send()` returns. Two retries arrive close together. What can happen?
o: Nothing: asyncio runs one task at a time, so the second waits for the first
The second raises KeyError because the key is being written
Both pass the not-in-dict check before either finishes, so it sends twice
The dict is locked during the await, so the second blocks
The loop cancels the second send as a duplicate
mcq.why: The await inside send lets the second task run between the first task's check and its write. Storing the future before awaiting closes the gap.

mcq.q: The caller says 'actually, Tuesday' while a slot lookup runs and the agent speaks a filler. Which handling is most defensible?
o: Cancel both and replay the original request with Tuesday added
Ignore the speech until the tool finishes, then ask again
Let the filler finish so the caller knows they were heard
Cancel the speech at once, and handle the new utterance while the read finishes or is dropped
Cancel the lookup but keep speaking so there is no dead air
mcq.why: Speech always yields to the caller. A read is harmless to finish or discard; the new utterance is the next turn and may change the request.

mcq.q: Why time events with time.monotonic() instead of time.time() in the orchestrator?
o: monotonic never goes backwards, so a clock adjustment cannot corrupt a latency
monotonic has nanosecond resolution on every platform
time.time() blocks the event loop while it reads the clock
monotonic is synchronized across processes, so logs line up
time.time() has one-second resolution on Linux
mcq.why: Wall-clock time can jump with NTP or manual changes. A monotonic clock only moves forward, which is what a duration needs.

Monotonic timestamps on every event so the timing is visible
