topics.title: The design, drawn cold
topics.brief: Two doors lead into one LiveKit room per call: phone over a SIP trunk, web over WebRTC. A Python worker on livekit-agents joins the room and runs the agent. The nuance people miss is trust: the worker is not given the backend, only an authorize function that hands it a short-lived, scoped token that can never send on the user's behalf.
points: Two doors: phone calls arrive over a SIP trunk into LiveKit, web calls over WebRTC; both land in one room per call
Worker: a Python process on livekit-agents is dispatched into the room and runs the agent
Authorize: the worker's only door to the backend, on a short time budget; it returns a short-lived, scoped token
Token scope: enough to read and draft, never to send on the user's behalf
Tools: every tool runs through an execution layer with idempotency on writes
Arrows: label what crosses each one (signalling, audio, a token, a tool call); that is what the interviewer reads
production: LiveKit SIP turns an inbound call from a SIP trunk into a participant in a room, so phone and browser callers look the same to the agent
LiveKit agent dispatch sends a worker job into the room when the call starts, instead of the worker polling for work
Short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens are the standard way to give a less trusted runtime access: a leak is bounded by scope and minutes
MockFlow-AI, his second voice system, was built from scratch on the same LiveKit base: sub-400ms end to end, Deepgram Nova-2 for speech, Silero for voice activity

mcq.q: Why does the worker get a short-lived, scoped token from an authorize function instead of a service key to the backend?
o: Service keys cannot be used from a Python worker
A misbehaving or compromised worker can do only what the token allows, and only for minutes
LiveKit requires a fresh backend token before audio can flow
The token caches the user's data, so tool calls get faster
It lets the worker skip checking who the caller is
mcq.why: The worker runs model-driven code on a live call. Scoping its access to a narrow, expiring token bounds the damage of any bug or compromise.

mcq.q: What does one room per call give the design?
o: A shared channel where one agent hears every call and multiplexes them
A recording store that replaces the call record
A queue that holds calls until a worker frees up
An isolated session per call that the worker joins, so calls share no state
A separate SIP trunk endpoint for every phone number
mcq.why: The room is the unit of isolation: one call's audio, participants and agent live together, and a failure stays inside that call.

mcq.q: Phone and web calls arrive by different routes. Where should they converge?
o: At the room: SIP and WebRTC both become participants, so one worker path serves both
At the model: each door runs its own agent with a shared prompt
At the database: each door writes transcripts and a job merges them
At the SIP trunk: web calls are converted to phone calls first
At the authorize function, which proxies the audio to the worker
mcq.why: Converging at the media layer means one agent, one tool path and one test surface, whatever the door.

open.q: Draw the voice agent you own on the whiteboard. What crosses each arrow, and where is the trust boundary?
open.probe: Whether he knows his own system cold, including why the boundaries are where they are.
a: Phone over a SIP trunk and web over WebRTC, into one LiveKit room per call
A Python worker on livekit-agents is dispatched into the room
The worker's only door to the backend is the authorize function, on a short budget
It gets a short-lived, scoped token: read and draft, never send
Tools go through an execution layer with idempotency on writes

say: I own alfred_'s voice agent end to end. Phone calls come in over a SIP trunk into LiveKit, web calls over WebRTC, and every call gets its own room.
A Python worker on livekit-agents joins the room and runs the agent.

The part I'd point at is the trust boundary. The worker only talks to the backend through an authorize function, and what it gets back is a short-lived token that can never send anything on the user's behalf.
avoid: Quoting user counts or traffic: describe what it is sized for

topics.title: One call, and the write path
topics.brief: Walk one call aloud: dispatch, authorize, greet, the turn loop, a write, the end. The nuance is that writes are where a voice agent hurts people. A half-heard instruction must never become an action, so the agent drafts, reads it back, waits for a yes, and the execution layer makes a retry replay instead of acting twice.
points: Start: dispatch into the room, authorize inside its budget, then greet
Turn loop: detect the end of the caller's turn, answer, run tools through the execution layer with a timeout and a filler
Write path: draft, read back the key fields, the person confirms, then it executes once
Code floors: the confirm flow is enforced in code, so the model cannot talk its way past a confirmation
Idempotency: a retried write returns the first result instead of acting again
Hang-up: with nothing executing before a yes, a call that drops mid-write leaves at most an unconfirmed draft
production: Read-back before commit is the norm in phone banking and ordering: restate the fields that matter, then ask for an explicit yes
Idempotency keys as payment APIs use them: the first result is stored under the key and returned for every retry
MockFlow-AI keeps the flow in code too: the conversation moves through stages in a state machine, and the model can only move it by calling a transition tool
A filler on slow tools and a hard timeout on every tool keep silence short while work runs

mcq.q: A caller says 'send it' after a half-heard request. What makes the design safe?
o: The model is prompted to be careful before sending
Low transcription confidence blocks the send
The send waits 30 seconds so the caller can cancel
A second model reviews every send before it goes
The agent can only draft; it reads the draft back and executes once after a yes
mcq.why: Safety comes from the shape of the path, not from asking the model to be careful: no action exists until a restated draft is confirmed.

mcq.q: The network drops right after the execution layer performed a write, and the worker retries. What happens?
o: The write happens twice, and a cleanup job removes the duplicate
The retry fails, and the agent apologizes to the caller
The retry carries the same key, so the first result comes back and nothing happens twice
The worker asks for confirmation again, then writes again
The user's account is locked until a person reviews it
mcq.why: Confirmation stops wrong actions; idempotency stops repeated ones. A retry with the same key replays the stored result.

mcq.q: The caller hangs up between the read-back and the yes. What is the right end state?
o: Execute it, since the caller heard the read-back
Nothing executed; at most an unconfirmed draft remains
Execute after a timeout unless the caller calls back
Queue it for the main agent to send later
Delete every trace of the draft so nothing leaks
mcq.why: Silence is not consent. Without a yes nothing runs, and the draft is there if the person wants to finish it later.

open.q: Walk me through one call on your agent, from the phone ringing to hang-up. Then: what stops it acting on a half-heard instruction?
open.probe: Whether he can narrate the flow in order and knows where the safety lives.
a: Dispatch into the room, authorize within its budget, greet
Turn loop: end of turn, answer, tools through the execution layer with timeout and filler
A write is a draft, read back, confirmed, then executed once
Confirmation is enforced in code; retries replay through idempotency
A hang-up before the yes leaves only a draft

say: The call is dispatched into its room, the worker authorizes, and it greets. Then it's a loop: wait for the end of the turn, answer, call tools when it needs them.
Writes are the part I'm careful about. The agent drafts, reads it back, and only after the person says yes does it execute, and the execution layer makes a retry replay instead of acting twice.
So a half-heard 'send it' can't turn into an email. The confirmation lives in code, not in the prompt.
avoid: Saying the prompt makes it safe: the safety is in code, and they will ask what happens when the model ignores the prompt

topics.title: The lean agent and the main agent in parallel
topics.brief: A lean agent answers on the call while the main agent works the same request in parallel, so the caller hears something fast and the heavy work still happens. The alternative, letting the lean agent escalate by tool call, adds a model round trip on exactly the turns that are already slow. The price is a background run on every turn and the work of tying two runs to one turn.
points: What: each turn goes to the lean voice agent and to the main agent at the same time
Why: an escalation tool call costs an extra model round trip, on the turns that are already slowest
Reads: whichever agent has the answer first speaks
Writes: they wait for the main agent's draft and the person's confirmation
Costs: a background run on every turn, correlating two runs, what to say during a long wait, and delivering a result after a hang-up
production: LiveKit's tool design guidance: keep tools fast under voice latency, and keep the caller informed while slow work runs
It is speculative execution: start work before you know it is needed and discard it if not, the same trade as hedged requests
At ten times the traffic: start the main agent only for intents that can need it, or cancel it once the lean agent has answered
Correlation: carry one turn id through both runs, so a late answer lands on the right turn or is dropped

mcq.q: Why send every turn to both agents instead of letting the lean agent call an escalation tool when it needs help?
o: An escalation tool call adds a model round trip on the turns that are already slowest
The lean agent cannot call tools at all
Running both agents halves the total model cost
The main agent cannot be reached through a tool call
Parallel runs make the lean agent's own answers more accurate
mcq.why: Escalation means the lean agent must first decide, then call, then wait. Starting the main agent at once removes that serial step where latency hurts most.

mcq.q: What is the main cost of running both agents on every turn?
o: Twice the audio bandwidth per call
The caller hears two voices answering
Writes can execute twice
A background run on every turn, including the ones the lean agent handles alone
Time to first audio doubles
mcq.why: Only one agent speaks and writes go through confirmation and idempotency. What you pay for is wasted background work on easy turns.

mcq.q: Traffic grows tenfold. What is the first change you would make to the parallel design?
o: Drop the lean agent and send every turn to the main agent
Make the main agent wait for an escalation tool call
Add a third agent to choose between the two answers
Cache every main agent answer per caller
Start the main agent only for intents that can need it, or cancel it once the lean agent answers
mcq.why: That keeps the latency win on hard turns while removing most of the wasted background runs on easy ones.

open.q: Why does your voice agent run two agents on every turn? What does it cost, and how would you change it at ten times the traffic?
open.probe: Whether he can defend a design choice and its costs, not only describe it.
a: What: the lean agent and the main agent both get every turn
Why: escalating by tool call adds a model round trip on the slow turns
Policy: reads, first answer wins; writes wait for the main agent and a confirmation
Cost: a background run per turn, correlation, long waits, results after hang-up
At scale: gate the main agent by intent, or cancel it once the lean agent answers

say: Every turn goes to a lean agent on the call and to the main agent at the same time. The caller hears something fast, and the heavy work still happens.
The other way is to let the voice agent escalate with a tool call, but that adds a model round trip on exactly the turns that are already slow.
It isn't free. There's a background run on every turn, even the easy ones, so at more traffic I'd only start the main agent for intents that can need it. That's the trade I'd make again.
avoid: Giving a seconds-saved number as measured: describe the reason, not a figure you cannot back

topics.title: Sizing, on a whiteboard
topics.brief: Start from calls, not users. Calls in the peak hour times average duration gives calls at once (Little's law); a burst factor goes on top; then a load test sets calls per worker, and that sets replicas. The nuance: the limit is usually CPU per call and model provider rate limits, not servers, and his own system is described by what it is sized for, never by traffic.
points: Little's law: calls at once equals arrival rate times average duration
Peak hour: size for the busiest hour (often 10 to 15% of the day's calls), not the daily average
Burst: multiply the peak-hour average by a burst factor of about 3 to 4 for minute-level spikes
Per worker: each call does CPU work (audio, voice activity detection), so calls per container is load-tested, not guessed
What breaks first: CPU per call, model provider rate limits, the authorize budget under load, and background runs from the parallel design
production: Commure reports one health system at 200K+ calls a year (vendor-reported): about 800 a working day, 120 in a 15% peak hour, about 6 at once at 3 minutes each, about 25 in a burst
Load test one worker with simulated calls until time to first audio or audio quality degrades; that point, not CPU percent, sets calls per container
Model providers limit requests and tokens per minute; a design with two agents per turn doubles requests, so it meets that limit first
Scale on concurrent calls per worker and keep warm spare capacity, since a cold container costs seconds on a live call

mcq.q: 120 calls arrive in the peak hour and average 3 minutes. On average, how many are live at once?
mcq.why: Arrival rate is 2 a minute; times 3 minutes is 6 (Little's law). Then add a burst factor before sizing.

mcq.q: Why size from calls in the peak hour rather than from daily active users?
o: Concurrency comes from arrival rate and duration, and the peak hour sets the arrival rate
User counts are private, while call counts are not
Little's law only works with hourly data
Providers bill per call, not per user
Daily users understate load because each user calls several times
mcq.why: Users only matter through how many calls they make and when. The peak-hour arrival rate times duration is the number that fills workers.

mcq.q: What do you load-test to decide how many containers to run?
o: Requests per second on the authorize function
The model's tokens per second
Memory per container at idle
Daily calls per container
Calls per container before time to first audio or audio quality degrades
mcq.why: Voice workers fail by sounding bad before they fail by crashing, so the limit is the call count where the gates start to slip.

open.q: How would you size the infrastructure for a voice agent taking one health system's phone calls?
open.probe: Capacity thinking from first principles, with honest numbers.
a: Start from calls: Commure reports about 800 a working day for one system (vendor-reported)
Peak hour at about 15%: 120 calls; at 3 minutes, Little's law gives about 6 at once
A burst factor of about 4: about 25 at once
Load-test calls per container; at 8 a container that is 4, plus headroom
Watch CPU per call, provider rate limits and the authorize budget as it grows

say: I start from calls, not users. Take the busiest hour, multiply by how long a call lasts, and Little's law gives you how many are live at once.
For one health system at around 800 calls a day, that's about 6 at once in the peak hour and maybe 25 in a burst.
Then I'd load-test one worker to see how many calls it holds before audio slips, and that gives the replica count. For the agent I own I talk about what it's sized for, and the method is the same.
avoid: Quoting alfred_ user or call numbers: describe what it is sized for, and use the method

topics.title: Evals for a voice agent
topics.brief: A scenario harness tests the voice agent in three layers: text, audio and live, with gates on audio quality, time to first audio, barge-in and dead air. A configuration ships only if it clears every gate. The nuance: most voice failures are timing and audio, which a text-only eval cannot see, and real failures from production should come back as new scenarios.
points: Text layer: scenarios check the right tool with the right arguments, cheap enough to run on every change
Audio layer: synthetic caller audio through the real speech stack, where turn detection and transcription errors appear
Live layer: calls through the real phone path, the only place telephony and network behave like production
Gates: audio quality, time to first audio, barge-in and dead air as thresholds; a configuration that misses any gate does not ship
Failure loop: a production failure scanner finds the calls that went wrong, and each becomes a scenario
production: Gate on percentiles, not averages: a p95 time to first audio catches the slow calls people remember
Repeat each scenario several times: one passing run of a stochastic agent is not evidence
Simulated callers with background noise and network jitter catch failures that clean test audio hides
Behaviour that must happen on time, like a filler or a timeout, belongs in code, where a test can pin it, not in the prompt

mcq.q: Every text-layer scenario passes, but callers say the agent talks over them. Why did the evals miss it?
o: The text scenarios used a different model
Talking over a caller is a timing and turn-taking failure that only audio and live layers can see
The prompt differs between text and voice modes
Text scenarios run too fast, so slowing them would catch it
The scenarios were too short to include an interruption
mcq.why: Text mode has no audio, no voice activity and no end-of-turn detection, so barge-in and overlap cannot fail there.

mcq.q: Which failure would a text-layer scenario catch?
o: Two seconds of dead air while a tool runs
The agent keeps talking after the caller interrupts
Speech to text mishears a name in a noisy room
The agent calls the booking tool with the wrong date
Time to first audio creeps up after a provider change
mcq.why: Text scenarios test reasoning and tool use: which tool, with which arguments. Timing and audio need the other layers.

mcq.q: Configuration A scores higher on answer quality but fails the barge-in gate. Configuration B passes every gate with lower quality. Which ships?
o: A, because quality matters more than one gate
A, with a prompt line asking it to stop when interrupted
B, because a configuration must clear every gate before quality is compared
Both, splitting traffic to decide later
Neither, until the two barge-in scores are averaged
mcq.why: Gates are floors, not weights. A configuration that talks over callers is not a candidate however good its answers are.

open.q: How do you evaluate a voice agent, and what would block a release?
open.probe: Whether he knows voice evals differ from chat evals, and treats them as a release gate.
a: Three layers: text for tools and arguments, audio for the speech stack, live for the phone path
Gates on audio quality, time to first audio, barge-in and dead air
A configuration ships only if it clears every gate; quality is compared after
Percentiles, not averages, and several runs per scenario
A failure scanner on production calls feeds new scenarios back in

say: For the voice agent I own there's a scenario harness in three layers: text, audio and live.

Text catches the wrong tool or the wrong argument. Audio and live catch what actually goes wrong on calls, which is mostly timing: slow first audio, talking over people, dead air. Those are gates, and a change that misses one doesn't ship.
Then a failure scanner finds the bad calls in production, and those become new scenarios. That's the loop.
avoid: Quoting a scenario count, pass rate or call numbers you cannot back on the spot

modules.title: Designing a patient-call voice agent
modules.blurb: Design an AI agent for a health system's phone line in 45 minutes, with safe EHR write-back and a HIPAA-aware approach, then tell your story for Commure.

topics.title: Requirements and numbers first
topics.brief: Spend the first few minutes on scope and numbers: which call types the agent handles (scheduling, rescheduling, cancellations, confirmations, FAQs, intake), what always goes to staff, the call volume and the latency target. Then draw the path of one call before any box for scale. The requirement people miss: every call must be answered, so the design needs a path to a human when the agent fails.
points: Scope: scheduling, rescheduling, cancellations, confirmations, FAQs and intake; clinical questions go to staff
Every call answered: if the agent, a vendor or the EHR fails, the call falls through to a human queue, never to silence
Numbers: about 800 calls a working day for one system (Commure's figure) gives about 6 at once in the peak hour, about 25 in a burst
Latency: a target for time to first audio and turn latency, stated up front, because it shapes every later choice
Order: requirements, entities, API, then the path of one call, then two deep dives you choose
production: Commure's agents cover scheduling, rescheduling, cancellations, confirmations, FAQs and intake, integrated with the EHR and telephony in real time
A common split for a 45-minute round: about 3 minutes of requirements, 10 for the high-level design, the rest on two deep dives
Phone systems keep a fallback route for every failure (overflow to an agent queue or voicemail), and an AI front door needs the same

mcq.q: In the first three minutes of the design round, what should you pin down before drawing boxes?
o: Which model and speech vendors to use
The database schema for appointments
How many replicas to run at launch
Which call types are in scope, what goes to staff, and the volume and latency targets
Which FHIR version the health system's EHR supports
mcq.why: Scope, handoff and numbers drive everything after. Vendors, schemas and replicas are answers to questions you have not asked yet.

mcq.q: Why draw the path of one call before any box for scale?
o: Latency, dispatch, write-back and handoff all hang off that path
Interviewers grade the diagram by its first box
Scale is out of scope in voice design rounds
One call is enough to compute the replica count
It avoids having to discuss the EHR integration
mcq.why: The single-call path is the skeleton. Scale is the same path multiplied, and its weak points only show once the path is drawn.

mcq.q: Which requirement most changes the design if you miss it?
o: The agent should sound human
Calls should finish within two minutes
Every call should be fully automated
Transcripts should be searchable by staff
Every call must be answered, so failures fall through to a human queue
mcq.why: A patient line cannot go silent. That one requirement adds a fallback route, health checks on vendors and the EHR, and a staff handoff path.

open.q: Design a voice agent that answers a health system's patient calls. Start with requirements.
open.probe: Whether he scopes before building, and treats the human fallback as a requirement.
a: In scope: scheduling, rescheduling, cancellations, confirmations, FAQs, intake
Out: clinical questions and anything uncertain, handed to staff
Every call answered: a human fallback when anything fails
Numbers: about 800 calls a day, about 6 at once in the peak hour, about 25 in a burst
A latency target for first audio and turns, then the path of one call

say: I'd start with what the agent does and what it never does. Scheduling, changes, confirmations, FAQs and intake are in; anything clinical goes to a person.
Then the numbers. For a system at around 800 calls a day that's maybe 6 calls at once at peak and 25 in a burst, so this is a latency problem more than a scale problem.
And one requirement I'd say out loud: every call gets answered, so if anything breaks the call falls through to staff.
avoid: Jumping to vendor names before scope and numbers

topics.title: The high-level design
topics.brief: The call comes in over SIP into a room per call; a worker runs a fast agent on the call and a heavier agent in parallel; tools read and write the schedule through an integration layer in front of the EHR; a handoff path transfers to staff with a summary; every call leaves a record. The nuance: the agent never answers schedule questions from the model, only from a tool reading the EHR at call time.
points: Telephony: the health system's number routes over a SIP trunk into a room per call; a worker is dispatched into it
Agents: a fast agent answers on the call while a heavier agent works the same request in parallel
Tools: read slots, hold, book, cancel and look up FAQs, all through an integration layer, never from model memory
Integration layer: one booking interface for the agent, with an adapter per EHR behind it
Handoff: a warm transfer to staff with a short summary, so the patient does not repeat themselves
Call record: transcript, actions, outcome and timings, for audit and for improving the agent
production: Commure describes its agents as integrated with the EHR and telephony in real time, so the agent works from the live schedule
Warm transfer with a whispered or on-screen summary is standard in contact centres and cuts handle time for staff
An adapter per EHR keeps vendor differences (FHIR APIs, vendor scheduling APIs, HL7 v2 messages) out of the agent
In the agent he owns, the lean and main agents run in parallel so the caller hears something fast and the heavy work still happens

mcq.q: Where should the agent get open appointment times from?
o: The model's context, loaded with the week's schedule at call start
A tool that reads the EHR's schedule at call time
A nightly copy of the schedule cached in the worker
The model's memory of earlier calls
The patient portal, read during the call
mcq.why: Slots change by the minute. Reading them through a tool at call time keeps the answer true and keeps the model from inventing times.

mcq.q: Why put an integration layer between the agent's tools and the EHR?
o: The EHR only accepts calls from servers inside the hospital
It lets the model write queries against the EHR safely
Each EHR differs, so the agent sees one booking interface and adapters map it per vendor
FHIR is too slow for live calls, so the layer caches every booking
It removes the need for a business associate agreement
mcq.why: Health systems run different EHRs with different scheduling APIs. An adapter layer keeps the agent and its tests the same across them.

mcq.q: A caller asks something the agent should not handle. What does a good handoff look like?
o: A warm transfer to staff with a short summary, so the patient does not repeat themselves
End the call and text the clinic's number
Send the caller to a voicemail box for staff
Keep the caller talking while the model searches for an answer
A cold transfer to the main line, with the reason logged
mcq.why: The handoff is part of the product. A summary carried to staff saves the patient time and the staff member a second intake.

open.q: Draw the high-level design. Where does the schedule come from, and what happens when the agent cannot help?
open.probe: Whether the boxes are the right ones and the agent is grounded in live data.
a: SIP into a room per call; a worker dispatched into it
A fast agent on the call, a heavier agent in parallel
Tools through an integration layer to the EHR, read at call time
Warm transfer to staff with a summary when the agent cannot help
A record per call for audit and improvement

say: The call comes in over SIP into its own room, and a worker joins it. That's the same shape as the agent I own.
The agent never answers from memory. Slots come from a tool reading the EHR during the call, through a layer that hides which EHR it is.
When it can't help, it hands off warm, with a summary, so the patient isn't starting over.
avoid: Implying you have integrated an EHR: say how you would

topics.title: Booking without double booking
topics.brief: The write path is hold the slot, read it back, confirm, then commit with an idempotency key, so a retry or a hang-up never books twice. The nuance: many EHR scheduling APIs offer neither a hold nor idempotency keys. Then the read-back is a race you settle at commit, and the idempotency is a ledger you keep yourself, with a read before any retry.
points: Read back: date, time, provider and location are said to the patient before anything is written
No hold: if the API cannot hold a slot, re-check it at commit and offer the next one on conflict
Idempotency: key the commit on the call and the slot; if the EHR has no key support, keep your own ledger of attempts
Unknown outcome: after a timeout, read the patient's appointments before retrying, never write blind
Rules in code: visit type, new or established patient, provider and length decide valid slots, so the tool only offers those
production: FHIR R4 models scheduling with Schedule, Slot and Appointment resources; Epic, Oracle Health and athenahealth publish FHIR APIs, but scheduling write support varies by vendor and site
Where FHIR writes are missing, integrations fall back to the vendor's own scheduling APIs or HL7 v2 scheduling messages
Idempotency keys as payment APIs use them: the first result is stored under the key and returned for every retry
In the agent he owns, writes go through an execution layer with idempotency and are confirmed by the person first

mcq.q: The EHR's API cannot hold a slot, and the patient takes 20 seconds to confirm. What do you do at commit?
o: Book it anyway, since the read-back counts as a hold
Skip the read-back so the window is shorter
Book first, read back, and cancel if the patient says no
Block the provider's calendar for the length of the call
Re-check availability as part of the commit, and offer the next slot if it was taken
mcq.why: Without a hold, someone else can take the slot during the read-back. Checking at commit turns a silent double booking into a short apology and a new offer.

mcq.q: The booking request times out. What do you do before retrying?
o: Retry at once with a new idempotency key
Read the patient's appointments to see if it landed, and retry with the same key only if not
Tell the patient it failed and ask them to call back
Retry three times, then hand off to staff
Assume it booked and confirm it to the patient
mcq.why: A timeout means the outcome is unknown. A read settles it; a retry with the same key is safe; a new key or a blind retry risks a second booking.

mcq.q: Where should a rule like 'new patients need a 40-minute slot' live?
o: In the system prompt, so the model filters slots
In the FAQ knowledge base the agent searches
With staff, who fix wrong bookings afterwards
In code in the scheduling tool, which only offers valid slots
In the notes field for each provider in the EHR
mcq.why: A rule the model is asked to follow is a rule it can break. A tool that never offers an invalid slot cannot be talked out of it.

open.q: How do you make sure a retried or interrupted booking never double-books a slot, given EHR APIs that may not support holds?

topics.title: Keeping a patient call safe
topics.brief: Decide in code what the agent may do and hand everything else to a person: clinical questions, emergencies and anything it is unsure of. Verify who is calling before saying anything about their care. Under HIPAA, the audio, transcript and call record are PHI, so every vendor that touches them needs a business associate agreement. He has not built under HIPAA; this is how he would approach it.
points: Scope in code: an allowlist of actions; anything outside it, or below a confidence bar, goes to staff
Clinical line: symptoms and medical questions go to clinical staff; emergency words trigger an instruction to call 911 and a transfer
Identity: verify the caller (for example name and date of birth) before revealing or changing anything about their appointments
PHI: audio, transcripts and call records hold PHI; telephony, speech and model vendors that process them each need a business associate agreement
Minimum necessary: give the model and the logs only the PHI the task needs, and keep it out of application logs
Learn from calls: flag the calls that went wrong, turn them into test cases, and gate every change on them
production: HIPAA's Security Rule asks for access controls, audit controls and transmission security; encryption in transit and at rest is standard practice
Many model and speech providers offer business associate agreements and zero data retention terms for healthcare customers; only vendors under one touch call data
An audit trail of every action (who, what, when, from which call) is what a covered entity needs when a patient disputes a booking
Confidence bands: act when sure, confirm when unsure, hand off below the floor

mcq.q: A caller says they have had chest pain since this morning and want an appointment. What should the agent do?
o: Book the earliest slot, since that is the request
Ask follow-up questions to judge severity, then book
Tell them to call 911 if it is an emergency, and transfer to clinical staff
Answer from the model's medical knowledge, then book
Book the slot and flag it for a nurse to review later
mcq.why: Triage is clinical work. The agent's job is to recognise the signal, give the emergency instruction and get a clinician on the line.

mcq.q: Which of these is PHI under HIPAA?
o: A call recording in which a patient gives their name and reason for the visit
A clinic's public opening hours
Daily call counts with no identifiers
The agent's system prompt
The list of a clinic's providers and specialties
mcq.why: PHI is health information tied to an identifiable person. A recording with a name and a reason for visit is exactly that; aggregate counts are not.

mcq.q: You want to use a new speech-to-text vendor on patient calls. What must be in place first?
o: Patient consent on every call before any vendor is used
Nothing, if the vendor deletes audio within 30 days
Nothing, since transcription is not storage
An on-premises deployment, since HIPAA bans cloud vendors
A business associate agreement, because the vendor will process PHI
mcq.why: Any vendor that creates, receives or processes PHI on the health system's behalf is a business associate (or a subcontractor of one) and needs a BAA. HIPAA does not ban cloud vendors.

open.q: How would you keep a patient call from going wrong, and how do you handle PHI in this design?
open.probe: Patient-centred judgement, and whether he is honest about what he has and has not done.
a: Code decides what the agent may do; clinical, urgent and uncertain calls go to people
Answer from the schedule through tools, and confirm before any write
Verify identity before discussing a patient's care
Treat audio, transcripts and records as PHI: BAAs with every vendor, minimum necessary, no PHI in logs, an audit trail
Turn real failures into test cases and gate changes on them

say: Decide in code what the agent may do, and hand everything else to a person: clinical questions, anything it isn't sure of. Answer from the schedule through tools, never from the model's memory, and confirm a booking back to the patient before writing it.
Then learn from real calls: flag the ones that went wrong, turn them into test cases, and run every change against them before it ships. That's how I work at alfred_.
I haven't built under HIPAA, so I'd say how I'd approach it: the audio and transcripts are PHI, every vendor touching them needs a BAA, and the model and logs only see what the task needs.
avoid: Implying you have shipped HIPAA-regulated systems
Reciting HIPAA rule numbers you cannot explain under a follow-up
